subject: maths

moments.title: Al-Khwarizmi at the House of Wisdom
moments.body:
The Abbasid Caliph al-Ma'mun establishes the House of Wisdom in Baghdad as a centre of learning. Scholars translate Greek, Persian, and Indian works into Arabic and produce original research.

Al-Khwarizmi writes a treatise: 'Al-Kitāb al-mukhtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-jabr wa-l-muqābala' — 'The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing'.

He systematically solves linear and quadratic equations using algebraic manipulation. The word 'algebra' is from 'al-jabr' (completion/restoration — moving a negative term to the other side). 'Al-Khwarizmi' Latinised to 'Algoritmi' gives us 'algorithm'.
moments.takeaway: Algebra is born as a discipline. The methods, the name, and the word 'algorithm' all come from al-Khwarizmi.

moments.title: Hindu numerals in Arabic mathematics
moments.body:
Al-Khwarizmi also writes a treatise on Hindu arithmetic, introducing the Indian decimal place-value system (with zero) to the Arab world. The original Arabic text is lost; we know it only through Latin translations.

The numerals 0-9, plus the place-value system, become standard in Arab mathematics. This is the system that will eventually conquer the world.
moments.takeaway: Indian numerals enter the Arab tradition. The system that we now call 'Arabic numerals' is mostly Indian, transmitted via Arabic-speaking scholars.

moments.title: Robert of Chester translates al-Khwarizmi
moments.body:
Robert of Chester translates al-Khwarizmi's algebra into Latin in Toledo or nearby. The Latin Christian world begins to acquire Arabic mathematical knowledge through Spain and Sicily.

The Toledo School of Translators becomes a major channel for Arabic science to reach Europe. Aristotle's Greek works also come back to Europe via Arabic translations of Greek originals.
moments.takeaway: Arabic mathematics enters medieval Europe. The transmission is slow but transformative.

moments.title: Fibonacci's Liber Abaci
moments.body:
Fibonacci, having travelled in North Africa with his merchant father, learns Arabic arithmetic. He writes 'Liber Abaci' (Book of Calculation) to promote the new numerals and methods in Italy.

The book includes the Fibonacci sequence (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...) in a problem about rabbit populations. The sequence — a small footnote in his book — becomes one of his lasting legacies.

Merchants gradually adopt the new system, though European bureaucracies stick with Roman numerals for centuries longer.
moments.takeaway: Italian merchants adopt Arabic numerals first. Banking, accounting and modern commerce become possible at scale.

moments.title: Symbolic algebra emerges
moments.body:
François Viète (1591) introduces letters for unknowns AND known quantities — symbolic algebra. Descartes (1637) standardises the conventions we still use (x, y, z for unknowns; a, b, c for constants; exponential notation).

These conventions are part of the 'algebra' we now teach in schools. Al-Khwarizmi's prose-based algebra has been largely superseded — but the methods are the same.
moments.takeaway: Algebra becomes symbolic in 17th-century Europe. The rhetorical algebra of medieval texts gives way to formulas.

now.title: Algebra today
now.body:
Algebra is the language of mathematics. Linear algebra, abstract algebra (groups, rings, fields), algebraic geometry, commutative algebra, homological algebra — all descend from al-Khwarizmi's original effort to systematise solutions to equations.

Computer algebra systems (Mathematica, Maple, SymPy, Sage) automate vast portions of algebraic manipulation. Symbolic computation is essential to physics, engineering, and many areas of mathematics.
now.open_questions: Can we automate higher-level algebra reasoning beyond what current systems do? What's the right balance between symbolic and numerical methods? Are there algebraic structures we haven't yet discovered that would simplify current problems?

reflection: Algebra is named after an Arabic word; algorithm is named after an Arabic name; our numerals were transmitted through Arabic mathematics. Yet many Western histories of mathematics jump from Greece to Renaissance Europe, omitting the Islamic Golden Age. What does it mean for a discipline to know its history honestly? And how should mathematical education reflect the global, multicultural origins of the field?
